under physical condition. The following results were revised and in-
cooperated to the results part on Page 7: “Their Achilles, patellar, and tail
tendons appeared hypoplastic and more translucent compared with controls.
Additionally, histology showed reduced collagen density and fewer cells in Reln-
/- mice tendons relative to controls (Fig. 3A and Fig. S4B).”and Page 8-9：“To
specifically assess the role of LEC-derived Reelin in tendon regeneration, we
selectively deleted Reln in LECs using Prox1-CreERT2; Relnfl/fl (RelnCKO) mice.
The expression of Reelin secreted by LECs were dramatically reduced in
tendon of Prox1-CreERT2; RelnCKO mice (Fig. S5A). Under baseline conditions,
RelnCKO and control Achilles tendons showed no significant morphological or
histological differences (Fig.4A–4D).”
We apologize for the confusion caused by including the injury group in Fig. 3C,
which was intended to demonstrate the successful establishment of the Achilles
transection model. To eliminate this confusion, we have deleted this group.
The histological images in Figure 3A and 3C have been replaced with higher-
quality versions at lower magnification to enhance clarity and improve
visualization of key details.
Moreover, the following sentences were added in the Discussion part on
Page 14-15: “In Reln-/- mice, newly formed tendons displayed reduced
cellularity, disorganized collagen fibers, and impaired mechanical properties.
Consistent with prior reports of Reln-/- mice exhibiting neural defects and weight
gain failure[42], we also observed tendon developmental dysplasia, reduced
lymphatic formation in Reln-/- mice. A previous study noted reduced smooth
muscle cell coverage and irregular diameters in lymphatic collecting vessels in
Reln-/- mice, despite normal lymphatic capillaries[43]. Collectively, these
findings suggest that the mechanisms controlling lymphatic vessel formation
and tendon development may differ by tissue microenvironment and could be
influenced by nervous system defects or growth impairments in Reln-/- mice. To
test the direct role of LEC-derived Reelin, we deleted Reln in lymphatics using
Prox1-CreERT2 mice. The resulting RelnCKO mice exhibited impaired tendon
regeneration despite normal tendon development and lymphatic formation,
confirming that lymphatic-derived Reelin specifically regulated tendon
regeneration. In vitro assays further verified the critical role of Reelin in
maintaining TSPC stemness.”
7. Some histology is of such high magnification that is lacks value (e.g. Fig 4).
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions. The histological
images in Figure 3A, 3C, 4C, 5K, 7F and Figure S 9G have been replaced with
higher-quality versions at lower magnification to enhance clarity and improve
visualization of key details.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
NCOMMS-25-23311, Chen et al., Lymphatic - Stem Cell Crosstalk Controls
Tendon Regeneration via Notch1-Srebp2 Mediated Cholesterol Metabolism
Lymphatic vessels drain tissue fluid and lipids and, also, traffic leukocytes.
Recent publications have indicated contribution of the lymphatics in the
intestinal, cardiomyocyte and hair follicle stem cell niche. In part, this paracrine
function is taken care by lymphatic endothelial reelin (Liu et al. 2020, Nature).
In their manuscript, Chen et al. investigate Achilles and patellar tendon in
postnatal and adult mice in homeostasis and upon injury. The authors use a
variety of methods, such as scRNA sequencing, lineage tracing, cell type-
specific gene deletions, and in vitro assays of cell differentiation and signalling.
Based on these, Chen et al. claim that they have “identified lymphatic vessels
as key components of tendon regenerative niche”. Further, they state that this
effect is caused by lymphatic endothelial reelin-induced NOTCH-signalling in
the tendon stem cells.
The study covers a huge area from identification of the essential cell types in
tendon regeneration to molecular mechanisms of tendon stem cell niche and
tendon regeneration. However, the provided data lacks many essential controls
and the motivation for the sequence of experimentation is not always obvious
to the reader. Especially, it is not clear whether there are lymphatic vessels in
the tendons. My major comments are listed below.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s positive comments and
valuable suggestions.
1. This manuscript and Tempfer et al (2015, Histochem. Cell Biol.) and Tong et
al. (2023, J. Orthop. Translat.) describe the existence of lymphatic endothelial
markers in the tendon tissue. However, these markers are also expressed in
other cell types such as muscle cells, neurons and blood vessels.
In this manuscript, Chen et al. characterize these structures mostly with Prox1-
TdTomato reporter mice. The provided images do not allow evaluation of
whether the depicted structures are lymphatic vessels. For example, the
structures shown in Fig. 2B-C resemble rather blood vessels or neurons than
lymphatic vessels. Also, in figures 2H-I, lymphatic markers are displayed at the
edge of the tissue, possibly reflecting a staining artifact, and do not show any
vessel-like morphology. In some of the figures, the staining is dot-like, for
example, Fig. 2A, 2H, S2G-I, and S5N. VE-cadherin staining, which should
exclusively highlight lymphatic endothelial and endothelial junctions, shows a
homogenous signal in the whole cell (Fig. S2D) and PROX1, which should be
nuclear is, does not display nuclear localisation (Fig. 2H).
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions. In response
to the reviewer’s concern regarding the structure of lymphatic vessels and
the dot-like staining pattern of lymphatics observed using Prox1-CreERT2
tdTomato reporter mice, we have conducted additional experiments.
Specifically, we performed immunolabeling with the vascular endothelial
marker CD31, alongside two distinct lymphatic vessel markers (LYVE1 and
VEGFR3), to further characterize lymphatic vessel morphology. We also
validated the structural integrity and functionality of these lymphatic vessels
using indocyanine green (ICG) and Evans blue tools that enable functional
assessment of lymphatic drainage. Furthermore, to enhance clarity and
support our observations, we have replaced the original figures with higher-
quality images and revised the corresponding results section to incorporate
these new findings and improved visualizations on Page 6-7: “To test whether
tendons contain lymphatic vessels, we used Prox1-CreERT2; tdTomato mice and
performed whole-mount imaging of the Achilles and Patellar tendons. This
approach enabled visualization of Prox1-Tdtomato-positive lymphatic vessels
in tendons (Fig.2A, 2B and Video1, 2). To validate their identity, we performed
immunolabeling using vascular endothelial and lymphatic vessel markers.
Prox1-Tdtomato-positive lymphatic structures co-expressed the vascular
endothelial marker CD31 and the LECs marker LYVE1 (Fig. S2B-S2D).
Because vascular endothelial growth factor C (VEGF-C)/VEGF receptor 3
(VEGFR3) signaling is essential for lymphatic development and
maintenance[25, 26], we also demonstrated VEGFR3 expression in Prox1-
Tdtomato- positive lymphatic vessels via immunostaining (Fig. S2E). Moreover,
for the interstitial fluid drainage function validation of these structures, we
injected indocyanine green (ICG) and Evans blue to trace lymphatic flow.
Subcutaneous ICG injections into the footpad showed uptake in Achilles
tendons within 30 min as well as time-dependent clearance (Fig. S2F). Evans
blue accumulated in Prox1-Tdtomato-positive vessels and also cleared over
time, confirming the distribution of functional lymphatics in tendons (Fig.
S2G)[27, 28].
Next, to test lymphatic responses to tendon injury, we established an Achilles
tendon transection model. Lymphatic vessels expanded significantly after 7
days injury in neonatal and adult mice, with increased Prox1-Tdtomato-positive
and LYVE1-positive lymphatic vessels (Fig. 2C, 2D and Fig. S2H, S2I).
Quantitative analysis confirmed significantly elevated Prox1 and Lyve1 mRNA
expression after tendon injury (Fig. S2J). To confirm the specificity, we treated
injured tendons with VEGFR3-blocking antibody, which inhibited LYVE1-
positive lymphatic vessel expansion (Fig. S2K). To model chronic tendinopathy,
we induced Achilles tendon overuse. In this model, lymphatic expansion also
occurred, as shown by confocal imaging of Prox1-positive vessels (Fig. S2L).
Together, these results demonstrate that both acute and chronic stress drive
lymphatic expansion in tendons.”
As immunofluorescence staining of sections, it is technically challenging to
visualize entire lymphatic vessels in a single-layer view. We have replaced high
quality of 3D confocal imaging in Fig 2A, Fig.2B, Fig 2C, Fig. S2G, Fig. S2H,
and Fig. S2L.
Regarding the PROX1 expression shown in Figure 2G: the sections were
derived from Prox1-CreERT2; tdTomato mice, and the signals depicted
correspond to tdTomato.
To solidify the existence of lymphatic vessels in the tendon and the basis for
this manuscript the authors should:
1.A. Provide high-resolution overview and Zoom in images to show the
lymphatic vessel lumen (optical orthogonal sections or 3D stacks). Also, the
localization of VE-cadherin and/or CD31 at cell junctions, and Prox1 in the
nucleus of the same cells should be shown.
Response: We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion. We have
replaced Figure 2A with high-resolution overview to show lymphatic vessel
using Prox1-CreERT2; tdTomato mice. To better delineate lymphatic vessel
distribution, we stained tendon tissues isolated from Prox1-CreERT2; tdTomato
mice with the vascular endothelial marker CD31 and lymphatic markers LYVE1
and VEGFR3. Additionally, we conducted co-staining of LYVE1 (a lymphatic-
specific marker) with CD31 to further characterize lymphatic vessel identity and
localization. The revised results incorporating these experiments have been
updated on Page 6: “To validate their identity, we performed immunolabeling
using vascular endothelial and lymphatic vessel markers. Prox1-Tdtomato-
positive lymphatic structures co-expressed the vascular endothelial marker
CD31 and the lymphatic endothelial marker LYVE1 (Fig. S2B-2D). Because
vascular endothelial growth factor C (VEGF-C)/VEGF receptor 3 (VEGFR3)
signaling is essential for lymphatic development and maintenance[25, 26],
we also demonstrated VEGFR3 expression in Prox1-Tdtomato- positive lymphatic
vessels via immunostaining (Fig. S2E).” and Page 6-7 “Next, to test lymphatic
responses to tendon injury, we established an Achilles tendon transection
model. Lymphatic vessels expanded significantly after 7days tendon injury in
neonatal and adult mice, with increased Prox1-Tdtomato-positive and LYVE1-
positive lymphatic vessels (Fig. 2C, 2D and Fig. S2H, S2I).”
1.B. Provide a functional draining assay (a tracer) to show that these structures
drain the tissue fluid (the tracer should be seen inside the lymphatic vessels).
Several time points should be included.
Response: Thank you for the valuable suggestion. For the functional
validation of lymphatic vessels in tendons, we employed indocyanine green
(ICG) and Evans blue as tools to visualize and confirm the presence of
functional lymphatic vessels. These newly generated experimental results
have been supplemented and incorporated on Page 6: “Moreover, for the
interstitial fluid drainage function validation of these structures, we injected
indocyanine green (ICG) and Evans blue to trace lymphatic flow. Subcutaneous
ICG injections into the footpad showed uptake in Achilles tendons within 30 min
as well as time-dependent clearance (Fig. S2F). Evans blue accumulated in
Prox1-Tdtomato-positive vessels and also cleared over time, confirming
functional lymphatics in tendons (Fig. S2)[27, 28].”
1.C. To show that the growth of these structures in development and upon
injury/inflammation is dependent on the VEGF-C to VEGFR3 signalling (the key
growth factor signalling route of lymphatics), authors should use one of the
established tools (blocking antibodies, VEGF-C ligand traps, or conditional
mouse strains).
Response: We appreciate your suggestions. To determine whether lymphatic
expansion following injury is dependent on VEGFR3 signaling, we conducted
analyses using a VEGFR3-blocking antibody. The newly generated
experimental results were added on Page 6-7: “Next, to test lymphatic
responses to tendon injury, we established an Achilles tendon transection
model. Lymphatic vessels expanded significantly after tendon injury in neonatal
and adult mice, with increased Prox1-Tdtomato-positive and LYVE1-positive
lymphatic vessels (Fig. 2C, 2D and Fig. S2H, S2I). Quantitative analysis
confirmed significantly elevated Prox1 and Lyve1 mRNA expression after tendon
injury (Fig. S2J). To confirm the specificity, we treated injured tendons with
VEGFR3-blocking antibody, which inhibited LYVE1-positive lymphatic vessel
expansion (Fig. S2K).”
2. Secreted reelin is expected to stay in the vicinity of the lymphatic vessels,
suggesting that tendon stem cells should be located close to the lymphatic
vessels. Authors should provide high-resolution double staining for the
lymphatics and the tendon stem cells and quantify the distance of the stem cells
from lymphatic in homeostasis and injury/inflammation (three independent
experiments are required). Also, authors should add a proliferation marker to
quantify, whether stem cells in the vicinity of the lymphatics have a higher
proliferative index than the ones further away.
The authors state that the lymphatics expand upon injury/inflammation. Would
this mean that only in these conditions do the lymphatics form the niche or, also,
during homeostasis?
Response: We appreciate your suggestions. We conducted double staining
for the lymphatics and tendon stem cells to analyze the regulating effects of
lymphatic vessels on tendon stem cells. The results were added on Page 10:
“Histological spatial analysis showed more Vldlr+ TSPCs located near lymphatic
vessels, with this localized abundance increasing after tendon injury.
Additionally, compared with Vldlr+ TSPCs distant from lymphatic vessels, those
adjacent ones showed a significantly higher proliferation index. Moreover, the
proliferation of Vldlr+ TSPCs was increased after injury compared with control
ones. (Fig. S6C-S6F). In RelnCKO mice, the proliferation of Vldlr+ cell was also
reduced (Fig. 5L), implicating lymphatics as a signaling hub maintaining Vldlr+
TSPC properties. To further validate Reelin's effects on TSPCs, TSPCs was
treated with recombinant Reelin protein ….”
Furthermore, to state the role of lymphatics during physical and pathological
conditions, the following sentences were added in the Discussion part on
Page 14-15: “It’s reported that crypt lymphatics preserve intestinal stem cell
stemness while inhibiting their premature differentiation[14], and skin
lymphatics support hair follicle stem cells while contributing to skin regeneration
and repair[40]. These observations indicates that lymphatics act as stem cell
niches under physiological and pathological conditions[41]. However, the
specific function and underlying mechanism are tissue dependent and need
further investigation. Our findings highlight Reelin from LECs as a key regulator
of TSPC stemness and differentiation. Following injury, Reelin expression in

supporting tendon repair.”
3. Authors use Prox1CreERT2 to delete conditional allele of reelin. Authors
should show that the reelin signal is lost in lymphatics upon tamoxifen induced
reelin deletion.
Response: Thanks for your suggestions. The deletion of allele of reelin in
Prox1CreERT2；Relnflox/flox was analyzed by immunofluorescence staining and
the results were added in Figure. S5A
4. If reelin affects the growth and/or maintenance of lymphatics (Fig. S4G-H
and S5N) it is difficult to judge whether the effect of reelin deletion on tendon
stem cells is directly caused by the reduced reelin amount or by the absence of
other lymphatic paracrine signals in vivo. Authors should discuss this in their
manuscript.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. We repeated the staining
for the lymphatic markers LYVE1 and VEGFR3 in Reln-/- and Relncko tendons
with their corresponding controls and the results were revised on Page 8:
“Expression of the lymphatic markers VEGFR3 or LYVE-1 was also reduced in
Reln-/- tendons compared with controls (Fig. S4G and S4H)” and Page 9:
“VEGFR3 and LYVE1 expression in RelnCKO tendons showed a slight but
nonsignificant decrease (Fig. S5D).”
Moreover, the following sentences were added in the Discussion part on Page
15: “Our findings further underscore the pivotal role of Reelin in regulating the
stemness and differentiation of TSPCs. Following injury, Reelin expression in
tendon lymphatics increased, functioning as a lymphoangiocrine signal
supporting tendon repair. In Reln-/- mice, newly formed tendons displayed
reduced cellularity, disorganized collagen fibers, and impaired mechanical
properties. Consistent with prior reports of Reln-/- mice exhibiting neural
defects and weight gain failure[42], we also observed tendon developmental
dysplasia, reduced lymphatic formation in Reln-/- mice. A previous study noted
reduced smooth muscle cell coverage and irregular diameters in lymphatic
collecting vessels in Reln-/- mice, despite normal in lymphatic capillaries[43].
Collectively, these findings suggest that the mechanisms controlling lymphatic
vessel formation and tendon development may differ by tissue
microenvironment and could be influenced by nervous system defects or
growth impairments in Reln-/- mice. To test the direct role of LEC-derived
Reelin, we deleted Reln in lymphatics using Prox1-CreERT2 mice. The resulting
RelnCKO mice exhibited impaired tendon regeneration despite normal tendon
development and lymphatic formation, confirming that lymphatic-derived
Reelin specifically regulated tendon regeneration. In vitro assays further
verified the critical role of Reelin in maintaining TSPC stemness.”
5. The authors use lymphadenectomy as described on rows 642-647. Here
the authors execute “a combined popliteal and superficial inguinal lymph node
excision”. Does this mean that the lymph nodes and the collector vessel in
between are removed? Then the tendon lymphatics are probably still in place
but the lymphatic drainage is disrupted. Authors should show, what happens
to tendon lymphatics upon lymphadenectomy (are they still present in the
tendon), does lymphadenectomy alter tendon drainage (see point # 1B) and
would loss of drainage affect the paracrine function of the lymphatics (for
example, acute reelin expression by the tendon lymphatics).
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestions. The
experiments investigating the effects of lymphatics on tendon regeneration,
using a lymphadenectomy model, were conducted prior to our acquisition of
Relncko mice. We acknowledge that the lymphadenectomy model has
limitations in clearly delineating the specific role of Reelin derived from LECs in
tendon regeneration. To enhance the rigor and clarity of our work, we verified
the effect of Reelin using Relncko mice, which were revised on Figure 4. We also
further analyzed lymphatic vessel distribution and lymphatic drainage function
following lymphadenectomy. To strengthen the logic of the manuscript, the
results using this model were presented in following attached Figure 1.
To investigate the effect of lymphatics on tendon healing, we performed
lymphadenectomy prior to inducing tendon injury. The results showed that the
lymphatic vessels were significantly decreased and distributed in an irregular
scattered manner, with impairment of lymphatic vessel drainage function after
lymphadenectomy (Attached Fig.1A-1C). The expression of Reelin were

Functionally, the lymphadenectomy group showed impaired tendon healing

index, HE and Masson trichrome staining (Attached Figure 1E, F). These
results indicated that the tendon regeneration capacity was impaired after
lymphadenectomy. However, the precise mechanism needs further
investigation.
Attached Figure 1 The tendon regeneration capacity was impaired after
lymphadenectomy (A) The lymphatic vessels and lymph node stained by Evans blue in control
and the Lymphectomy in mice limbs. (B) The expression of LYVE-1 in control and lymph group,
as assessed by immunofluorescence staining. (C) Representative ICG-NIR images of limbs
immediately (0 h),2h and 24 h and ICG 24h clearance after ICG injection in control and lymph
group. (D) The expression and semi-quantification of LYVE-1 and Reelin in control and lymph
group, as analyzed by immunofluorescence staining. (E) The footprints and AFI in the control,

analysis in the control, injury and lymph groups. (Control: the sham group, Repair: 4 weeks

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript, a functional crosstalk between lymphatic vessels and tendon
stem/progenitor cells (TSPCs) was found to play a critical role in tendon
regeneration. Mechanistically, Reelin secreted by lymphatic endothelial cells
(LECs) promoted phosphorylation of DAB1 through interaction with VLDLR in
TSPCs. The activated DAB1 subsequently triggered a Notch1-SREBP2-
mediated cholesterol metabolism pathway, which proved essential for
maintaining TSPC stemness. This study reveals a novel lymphatic-tendon
signaling axis and demonstrates its physiological relevance in tendon
regeneration. The authors provided substantial experimental validation through
rigorous in vitro and in vivo approaches. Although Reelin-DAB1-Notch1-
SREBP2 signaling has been previously characterized in cardiac and intestinal
tissues, this work represents the first elucidation of its mechanistic role in
tendon biology. Given these findings, we recommend this manuscript for
publication in Nature Communications, pending clarification of the following
points:
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s positive comments.
1. Discrepancies exist between the textual descriptions and annotations in
Figure 5.

has undergone thorough revision and rigorous proofreading to ensure the
textual descriptions and annotations in Figure 5 are consistent and accurate.
2. Comprehensive documentation of human tendon samples is required,

temporal parameters of sample collection post-injury.

the human tendon samples used in this study were added in the Methods
section on Page 21: “For human tendon samples and three pathologic tendon

obtained from published datasets (SRA: PRJNA975881, PRJNA976191),

injury etiology being tendon injury. Detailed sample metadata, including exact
age, sex, disease status, and precise time points of collection, were provided

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have provided extensive new data. A few additional comments regarding revised Figure 1 are below.
Fig 1 -
- 1B, comparison between neonate and adult could also be provided by UMAP

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have improved the manuscript, for example, the methodology section is improved (point #6 in the original statement), quantification of a western blot is added (#8 ) and interpretation of the lymphadectomy experiment has been modified (#5).
However, the major concern still exists: are the lymphatics within the tendon, as stated by the authors, or superficial, i.e. growing on top of the tendon? This is a major concern and affects the interpretation of the results presented in this manuscript.
1. The authors now show a draining assay (Fig. S2F-G) and state that “… showed uptake in Achilles tendons within 30 min as well as time-dependent clearance (Fig. S2F).” However, only approximate localization of the signal in the leg is shown. There are non-tendon lymphatic vessels in the leg that drain the footpad area. Thus, this assay does not show that there are functional/fluid-draining lymphatics within the tendon. The authors should show, for example, 3D imaging (a stack), showing lymphatic marker, a drainage tracer, and a tendon marker to show that draining lymphatics are within the tendon.
2. Authors provide better quality images and videos of lymphatics (for example, Fig. 2A-C, and videos) but it is not possible to interpret whether the lymphatics are truly embedded within the tendon or just grow on top of it (superficial). Authors should use 3D stacks or cross sections to show that lymphatics are within the tendon. Here, “a tendon marker” would make the interpretation of the images easier. Authors should also always indicate in the figure legend whether the shown images are a flattened projection of a stack or images of a sectioned tendon.
3. As expected, the authors show that the reelin signal is restricted to the direct vicinity of the stained lymphatic vessels (Fig. 2G-H). If lymphatic endothelial reelin directly controls tendon progenitor cells, then it would be expected that the progenitor cells reside next to lymphatic vessels. In response to point #2, authors show that upon injury, the distance of progenitor cells to lymphatic vessels is decreased (Fig. 6D), which is expected, since the density of the vessels is increased. The authors also show that within 100 micrometers from lymphatic vessels the KI67 positivity of VLDLR+ cells is higher. Authors should re-analyze their data and show a histogram of distances of KI67-positive VLDLR+ cells from lymphatic vessels and a histogram of distances of KI67-negative VLDLR+ cells from lymphatic vessels.
4. Many of the requested data are shown only as representative images, for example, reelin loss (Fig. S5A) and anti-VEGFR3 effect on lymphatic markers (Fig. S2K). In the Figure legends, it should be mentioned how many independent experiments the data represents. The anti-VEGFR3 data should be quantified (3 independent experiments). Also, the used anti-VEGFR3 antibody should be mentioned in the methodology section (the reagent list).
5. In response to point #4, now, the authors show that there is less lymphatic marker expression upon constitutive (Fig. S4G-H) and conditional loss of reelin (Fig. S5D) (a trend for the latter). It is possible that the tendon phenotype is caused, in part, by decreased amounts of lymphatic vessels and, thus, other lymphatic endothelial paracrine factors. This possibility should be clearly stated in the manuscript.
6. In response to point #7, the authors state that reelin affects both VLDLR expression (Fig. S7A) and direct APOE binding to VLDLR (Fig. S8A). There is no description of the latter experiment neither in the Figure legend nor in the method section. Please elaborate on how the pull-down was done. The authors should also clarify which ones of the multiple bands represent VLDLR and APOE and provide quantification of 3 independent experiments (normalization of the pulldown protein levels to input levels).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I have carefully reviewed the revised version of the manuscript entitled “Lymphatic–Stem Cell Crosstalk Promotes Tendon Regeneration via Notch1–Srebp2–Mediated Cholesterol Metabolism.”
General Assessment
The revised manuscript now presents a much clearer and coherent study demonstrating that lymphatic endothelial cell–derived Reelin orchestrates tendon stem/progenitor cell (TSPC) behavior through a VLDLR–DAB1–Notch1–SREBP2 axis, which is essential for tendon regeneration. The addition of new imaging, functional, and mechanistic data strongly supports the central hypothesis and improves the robustness of the conclusions. Overall, the quality of figures, histological evidence, and methodological descriptions has been markedly improved.
Remaining Minor Points for Consideration
Quantitative Data Presentation:
While the main findings are supported, a few quantitative comparisons (e.g., Vldlr⁺ cell proliferation near lymphatic vessels, Fig. S6F) could benefit from clearer statistical annotation in the figure panels for readers’ clarity.
Discussion Section:
The discussion could be slightly condensed by merging overlapping statements on developmental versus regenerative mechanisms to improve focus and readability.
Terminology Consistency:
Please ensure consistent use of “lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs)” rather than alternating with “lymphatic endothelium” or “lymphatics,” to maintain terminological precision across sections.
Summary Recommendation
The manuscript now provides a well-structured, mechanistically compelling, and visually convincing demonstration of lymphatic–stem cell interaction in tendon regeneration. The revisions have adequately addressed all major concerns raised in the previous review.

Major improvement is the co-staining of tendon and lymphatic markers (S2G and S2K-L, #1 and #2), which allows the evaluation of the major point: are the observed lymphatic vessels growing superficially on the tendon or are there lymphatic vessels in the tendon as stated by the authors (see the two previous statements). However, the interpretation of the results and the discussion should better reflect the provided data.
1. Now, authors demonstrate by co-staining of tendon and lymphatic markers that most lymphatic vessels grow superficially on the tendon, whereas there is only some lymphatic marker staining in/within the tendon in homeostasis (Figure S2K-L). Also, the number of lymphatic vessels increases upon injury (Fig. S2K-L).
a. In relevant locations in the manuscript, the authors should state clearly that most of the lymphatics grow superficially on the tendon and that the performed functional experiments cannnot make a clear distinction between the role of superficial or “within the tendon” lymphatic vessels.
b. The authors should clarify whether they have quantified in Fig. S2K-L only the LVs in/within the tendon or also the ones growing superficially on the tendon.
2. Now, authors show Evans blue together with lymphatic and tendon marker staining. In the manuscript, the authors write (p. 6) “Evans blue accumulated in LYVE1 positive lymphatic vessels of tendon tissues evidenced by COL1α1 staining, which was also cleared over time (Fig. S2G)[27, 28]. These results verified the distribution of functional lymphatic vessels in tendons”. However, in Figure S2G it is shown that Evans blue is in the lymphatic vessels that grow superficially on the tendon (at the outer border of the tendon) but it is unclear whether there is any Evans blue within the tendon in the lymphatic vessels. Authors should clearly state that there are functional lymphatic vessels that are located superficially on the tendon, whereas it is unclear whether there are functional lymphatic vessels within/in the tendon.
3. In the rebuttal letter (point #3) and manuscript (p. 11, rows 301-303) authors write “Moreover, the proliferating VLDLR positive cells were located relatively farther from lymphatic vessels than the non-proliferating cells (Fig. S6E-S6H).”, whereas they show in Figure S6H that the proliferating cells (Ki67+) are closer to lymphatics. Authors should clarify which one is correct.
The authors should, further, clarify whether they have quantified the VLDLR+Ki67+ distances only to the LVs in/within the tendon or also to the ones growing superficially on the tendon.
